Statement in support of
L.D. 904, An Act to Exempt from Fees Certain Services Performed by the Health and Environmental Testing Laboratory for Criminal Investigations
Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services
March 24, 2025
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and honorable members of the Health and Human Services Committee. My name is Jason Moen. I am the Chief of the Auburn Police Department, and the President of the Maine Chiefs of Police Association. I am submitting testimony on behalf of the Maine Chiefs of Police Association in support of LD 904.
The mission of the Maine Chiefs of Police Association is to secure a closer official and personal relationship among Maine Police Officials; to secure a unity of action in law enforcement matters; to enhance the standards of police personnel, police training and police professionalism generally; to devise ways and means for equality of law enforcement throughout the state of Maine; to advance the prevention and detection of crime; to prescribe to the Law Enforcement Code of Ethics; and to promote the profession of law enforcement as an integral and dedicated force in today's society sworn to the protection of life and property.
One of the most critical components of a drug investigation is the ability to analyze a confiscated substance to determine its legality. Until recently, these costs were recoverable through restitution as the expense was deemed necessary as part of an investigation of criminal activity. However, in 2021, the Legislature changed what constitutes a critical investigation expense eligible for restitution. Now, the costs of these tests are only recoverable if the defendant is convicted of trafficking a scheduled drug, and the court makes a finding that the conduct underlying the conviction was motivated by profit.
Last week, the Maine Chiefs of Police Association testified before the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee in favor of a proposal (LD 717) that would change this law to allow for the costs of these tests to be recoverable once again.

Since this new law has been in place, municipal law enforcement agencies have borne the cost of these drug analyses, which cost $155 per test, and they are putting a financial strain on our departments. For example, in Fiscal Year 2024, the Auburn Police Department spent $9,610 on drug testing, close to the average amount larger departments expect to incur annually for active testing years. For some of our smaller community departments that figure tends to be about half that amount, again, dependent on the testing volume.
One way to rein in these costs impacting municipal budgets is to eliminate the fee for drug analysis testing altogether. That is exactly what is proposed in LD 904. This bill includes a provision that there is no fee for the lab analysis of a substance that is suspected of being an illegal drug when such testing or analysis is conducted pursuant to a criminal investigation.
Municipal resources are stretched thin, and the costs associated with drug analyses burden tight budgets and municipal taxpayers even more. When local law enforcement units must cover the costs of these tests, other aspects of criminal investigations are impacted. Law enforcement agencies and prosecutors must decide where to spend limited resources, making it difficult to prosecute drug cases effectively. Removing the fee for these tests will eliminate the need to make these difficult decisions.
For these reasons, the Maine Chiefs of Police Association supports the passage of LD 904. We respectfully ask members of the Committee to vote Ought to Pass.

Testimony of the Maine Municipal Association
In Support of
LD 904, An Act to Exempt from Fees Certain Services Performed by the Health and Environmental Testing Laboratory for Criminal Investigations
March 24, 2025
Sen. Ingwersen, Rep. Meyer and distinguished members of the Health and Human Services Committee, my name is Rebecca Graham, and I am submitting testimony in support for LD 904, An Act to Exempt from Fees Certain Services Performed by the Health and Environmental Testing Laboratory for Criminal Investigations, at the direction of MMA's Legislative Policy Committee (LPC). Our LPC is made up of individuals from across Maine with municipal officials elected by their peers across Maine's 35 Senate districts representing communities with very different access to available enforcement resources and local capacity.
Laboratory testing to determine the presence of impairing levels of alcohol or other illegal substances is not only crucial to hold individuals accountable for criminal behavior associated with the need for the testing but also to protect the rights of individuals involved in the cases. Under the current law enacted in 2021, in limited circumstances where there is a nexus to profit motivated crime, restitution for the costs of some laboratory testing in criminal cases can be recovered through restitution. That is not the case for testing for most other criminal investigations where the flat fee of $155 per test is borne exclusively by the investigating agency. This has increased the costs for agencies making it more expensive to investigate criminal behavior that significantly harms the lives of others and not related to trafficking of drugs for profit. This includes crimes such as rape, murder, fatal accidents from impaired drivers, abuse and endangerment of children, domestic violence and other violent crime that may require testing of both the suspect and victims depending on the circumstances.
These victims deserve and need the support of state resources to address the basic costs to run a state laboratory and not rely on revenue generated from the cost of investigations paid by the investigating agency.
Municipal resources are already stretched thin and municipal and county police budgets, supported only through property tax, cannot adequately anticipate the realized costs of future investigations for crimes not yet reported or committed. The annual costs for such testing is adding an estimated $10,000 dollars to police budgets, but can easily exceed that budget line based on investigative needs. Criminal investigations should never be subjected to locally available or budgeted funds, and all-in revenue generation sources should be used to protect victims and state interest in criminal investigations.

For these reasons, municipal officials respectfully ask you to consider adequately resourcing the Health and Environmental Testing Laboratory for this purpose and shift the burden for laboratory testing for criminal investigations to broader based revenue sources and away from the property tax.

Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services on LD 904, An Act to Exempt Fees For Certain Services From the Health and
Environmental Laboratory for Criminal Investigations
March 27, 2025

Good afternoon, Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and esteemed members of the
Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services: I am Dave Haggan and I have
the honor of representing the people of Senate District 10, which includes three
municipalities in Hancock County and nine municipalities in Penobscot County. I am pleased to present LD 904, An Act to Exempt from Fees Certain Services Performed by the
Health and Environmental Testing Laboratory for Criminal Investigations.

In 2021, the 130th Legislature enacted LD 477, which severely limited the ability to seek
restitution for drug testing fees. This change was put forward because advocates believed that it would create an insurmountable barrier to recovery if someone convicted of possession, furnishing, or trafficking to have to pay restitution fees, unless that convicted person was motivated by profit.

Before this law took effect, investigating agencies, such as municipal police departments or county sheriff offices, could request restitution from a convicted party to recover the cost of
testing and analyzing of illegal drugs as part of a criminal investigation for trial. Now those
costs can only be requested if the court finds that the conduct underlying the conviction was motivated by profit.

Contrary to what many think, most traffickers in Maine are not primarily motivated by profit. Instead, they sell these dangerous and illegal substances to support their own habits. In order to find a trafficker truly motivated profit, you would have to look much higher up
the chain of organized crime.
This change, while noble in intent, has become and unfunded mandate on municipal and county police departments. In fact, between 2021 and January 2025, these analysis fees
have cost the Brewer Police Department more than $20,000. And regardless of the motivation, someone who traffics drugs is endangering our communities.

If we aren't willing to hold drug offenders accountable for the expenses associated with testing and analysis required to keep our communities safe, the state should pick up the tab.
This burden should not fall on our municipalities and counties.

Thank you for your time today. I would be happy to answer any questions but assure you there are people here today who know far more about this topic than I do. Thank you for
your consideration and I encourage you to vote "ought to pass" on LD 904.

Testimony of the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention
Maine Department of Health and Human Services

Before the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services

iiniiioppiositioin

904, An Act to Exempt fiom Fees Certain Services Performed by the Health

and Environmental Testing Laboratory for Criminal Investigations

Sponsor: Senator Haggan Hearing Date: March 27, `Z025

Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Health and Human Services, my name is Michael Duschenchuk, and I serve as the Forensic Technical Laboratory Director of the Maine Center for Disease Control (Maine CDC) in the Maine Department of Health and Human Services. I am here today to testify in opposition to LD 904, An Act to Exempt from Fees Certain Services Performed by the Health and Environmental
Testing Laboratory for Criminal Investigations.
As the title states, this bill intends to eliminate testing fees charged by Maine CDC - Health and Environmental Testing Laboratory (HETL) for samples related to criminal investigations. HETL
has a forensic chemistry section (FCS) that performs toxicology and seized drug testing and is the only forensic testing laboratory in the State of Maine providing these services. Over the past
four fiscal years, the FCS has generated an average revenue of approximately $599,827 from
testing fees related to criminal investigations, including expert testimony and generation of discovery materials.eAdditionally, if testing fees are eliminated for individual law enforcement
agencies and prosecutorial bodies, HETL-FCS anticipates a statistically significant increase in
the number of seized drug cases submitted for testing. If testing fees are removed, LD 904 is
expected to incur an additional annual cost of approximately $1.5 million, based on the anticipated loss of revenue and the additional staff and equipment needed to respond to the
increase in testing requests.

Currently, fees are detailed in the 10-144 CMR, Chapter 257, State of Maine Schedule of
Charges for Testing and Services Provided by the Maine Health and Enviromnental Testing Laboratory, last amended in 2020, and are as follows:
I Blood Alcohol testing - $70 per sample
0 Blood Drug testing - $225 per sample* o *The entire Blood Drug Testing Program is currently paid for through a Department of Public Safety-Bureau of Highway Safety Federal National Highway Traffic Safety Administration Grant Program which expires on
September 2025. At present, due to this federal funding source, HETL is not able
to generate revenue on any blood drug testing. Based upon the number of samples

received in 2024, blood drug testing would be expected to generate approximately

$225,000 annually in additional revenue.

0 ~Urine Drug testing'- $225 per sample T V

~- -

I Seized Drug testing - $155 per sample

Q Expert Testimony - $100 per hour

0 Discovery Materials - $50 for initial discovery request; $30 per hour for additional

requests

Evidence is submitted to HETL FCS by law enforcement agencies throughout the state in
connection with criminal investigations. Testing by FCS is performed in furtherance of prosecution of Class A-E crimes, including but not limited to, those described in Title 17-A and Title 29-A of Maine Revised Statutes. Requests for forensic seized drug testing are made
primarily through the prosecuting agency, with the cost of this testing borne by the submitting law enforcement agency. Forensic Toxicology testing fees are primarily covered by the Department of Public Safety Bureau of Highway Safety under Implied Consent/Duty to Submit.
These testing fees are used to supplement the HETL budget, purchase supplies, pay forensic personnel salaries along with other costs associated with the operations of the HETL Forensic
Chemistry Section.

There are two factors that must be considered if this bill is implemented and further explain why
Maine CDC is in opposition to LD 904, as currently written.

First, with the exemption of fees related to criminal investigations, it is expected that the amount of testing requests would increase significantly for the Seized Drug Testing Unit within HETL. With removal of these fees, prosecutors will no longer have to consider budgetary limitations when determining the type and overall number of samples within a case needed for a
prosecution. To address this expected increase in testing, the HETL Forensic Chemistry Section
will require additional chemist and evidence technician positions, analytical instrumentation and processing equipment as described in the attached fiscal note.

Second, this bill does not address the manner in which the revenue generated by these fees are to
be supplanted in order to keep the HETL Forensic Chemistry Section functional. Loss of this
revenue will require other funding source(s) to be identified to maintain not only the current level of testing, but the increase in testing expected if this bill were to be passed.

In conclusion, this bill seeks to remedy the issue of charging law enforcement and prosecuting
agencies forensic testing fees, but without identifying another funding source to keep the HETL
Forensic Chemistry Section operational, as well as adequately staffed and equipped.

Thank you for your time and attention. I would be happy to answer any questions you may have and to make myself available for questions at the work session.
